itemRequests.readingquiz: Write two ORIGINAL passages from my notes, about 300 words each: one short story and one nonfiction article. Both versions read the same two passages. 10 multiple choice per version, inference and text evidence, with Part A / Part B pairs where Part B asks for the quotation that best supports Part A. Then one short constructed response (RACE). The questions should really need the passage: last year my kids could guess half of a store-bought quiz without reading.
itemRequests.rubric: A 4-point RACE rubric (Restate, Answer, Cite, Explain) for the constructed response, in words my 7th graders can use to check their own answer.

order.requests: Mixed class: some readers are a year below grade level, so keep sentences clear but don't make the passages babyish. Number the paragraphs; my students cite them in brackets like [3].

passages.title: Biscuit
paragraphs: Mrs. Abara handed Kiran her spare key and a page of notes. "Biscuit is shy with new people, so don't take it personally," she said. At the bottom she had written: Dev will come Thursday to water the plants. Kiran had asked his parents for a pet for three years. Four days with Biscuit, Monday to Thursday, felt like a test, and he planned to get a perfect score.

On Monday morning the apartment was silent. Kiran filled the bowl and crouched by the couch. "Here, kitty, kitty!" he called. He shook the food bag and tapped the bowl with a spoon, louder each time. Nothing moved. He walked to school with his shoulders up near his ears.

That evening the bowl was empty, and the blanket on the armchair was warm and covered in orange hair. Kiran checked behind the mat. Nothing had spilled. At dinner his sister Tam said, "So she ate!" Kiran shook his head. "Dev must have come by and tossed it out. She won't touch anything I give her."

On Tuesday he tried harder. He waved a feather toy under the bed and sang to her. Two green eyes watched him from the dark, then slid away. "She misses Mrs. Abara too much to eat," he told Tam. "And she hates me." Tam shrugged. "Or you're really loud."
On Wednesday evening Kiran had a math test to study for and no energy for singing. He sat on the floor with his back against the couch and opened his notebook. He forgot to call her at all.

After a while, something warm leaned against his elbow. Biscuit sat beside him, staring at the page as if she were checking his work. Kiran did not reach for her. He kept writing, but slower, and he hardly breathed. She stayed until he finished the last problem.

On Thursday, Dev was watering the plants when Mrs. Abara got home. She glanced at Kiran's notebook on the table. "I used to teach math, you know." Kiran started to say, "She didn't eat at first," then looked at Dev and stopped. "Could I come over sometimes?" he asked instead. "I'd bring my homework." Mrs. Abara smiled and pressed a folded ten-dollar bill into his hand.

passages.title: The Long Fence
paragraphs: Across the dry middle of Australia runs a fence more than 5,000 kilometers long. It is called the Dingo Fence, and it is one of the longest structures on Earth. Ranchers began building it more than 100 years ago. They wanted to keep dingoes, Australia's wild dogs, away from their sheep.

The fence mostly works. Dingoes are common on one side and rare on the other. On the sheep side, ranchers also poison, trap and shoot wild dogs. Still, a few slip through gaps after floods. The fence gives scientists a natural experiment. Nobody set it up as a test, but scientists can compare places on the two sides that have the same kind of land and the same weather.

On the side with few dingoes, there are many more kangaroos. Dingoes hunt kangaroos, so where dingoes are rare, more young kangaroos live to grow up. In many places on that side, the grass is cropped short and the ground is barer. Kangaroos graze on the same grass that sheep need.

The changes go further. Red foxes and feral cats were introduced to Australia by people from Europe. Dingoes kill foxes and cats. Where dingoes are rare, foxes are more common, and small native animals, such as hopping mice, are harder to find. Some studies find more cats there too. Foxes and cats are a main reason many small Australian mammals have disappeared from large areas.

None of this makes the answer simple. Dingoes do kill sheep and calves. For the families who raise sheep, the fence protects their living. Some people say the fence should come down. Others say it must stay. Many scientists say more study is needed before anyone decides.
The fence was built to solve one problem: dingoes eating sheep. It shows how pulling one hunter out of a place can change far more than anyone planned.

questions.skill: infer a character's feelings or beliefs

prompt.A: In paragraph 4, what does Tam think is really keeping Biscuit away?
prompt.B: In paragraph 1, how does Kiran think of the four days he will look after Biscuit?

A: She misses her owner and will not eat.
Kiran makes too much noise around her.
She is shy around people she does not know.
The feather toy under the bed scares her.
B: a chance to have the pet his parents will not get him
a job Mrs. Abara warned him would be hard
a test he wants to do perfectly on
a way to earn the money he wants for a pet

why.A: Tam answers Kiran with "Or you're really loud" [4]. Missing Mrs. Abara is Kiran's own idea [4], not Tam's; "shy with new people" is what Mrs. Abara says [1]; the feather toy is only what Kiran waves [4].
why.B: "Four days with Biscuit ... felt like a test, and he planned to get a perfect score" [1]. He has wanted a pet for three years [1], but these four days do not give him one; Mrs. Abara says Biscuit is shy, not that the job is hard [1]; the money comes only at the end [7] and he never asks for it.

prompt.A: In paragraph 3, why does Kiran check behind the mat?
prompt.B: In paragraph 3, why does Kiran shake his head when Tam speaks?

A: He thinks Biscuit is hiding behind it where he can't see her.
He is looking for the spare key that Mrs. Abara gave him.
He wants to see whether Dev left a note for him under the mat.
He wants to know if the food fell out instead of being eaten.
B: He believes the food was thrown out and not eaten.
He does not want his little sister to tease him about the cat.
He thinks the cat spilled it.
He is sure she will not eat unless Mrs. Abara is home.

why.A: He finds the bowl empty and checks, then notes "Nothing had spilled" [3]; he does not believe she ate. Biscuit hides under the bed [4], not behind the mat; the key and the note about Dev came from Mrs. Abara [1].
why.B: He says "Dev must have come by and tossed it out" [3]. Tam teases him only on Tuesday [4]; he checked the mat and "Nothing had spilled" [3]; missing Mrs. Abara is his idea the next day [4], not his reason here.

prompt.A: Part A: In paragraph 7, why does Kiran stop in the middle of what he is saying?
prompt.B: Part A: Which statement about Dev is best supported by the story?

A: He does not want Mrs. Abara to think he failed the job.
He is afraid talking will scare Biscuit.
He sees that what he told Tam on Monday was wrong.
He does not want Dev to hear that he had trouble.
B: He is the reason Biscuit hid under the bed.
He came by each day of the week to water the plants.
He threw out Biscuit's food on Monday evening.
He did not come to the apartment until Thursday.

why.A: Two steps: on Monday Kiran told Tam that Dev tossed the food out [3], but the note says Dev comes Thursday [1], and Dev is only now there [7]. Seeing Dev, Kiran realizes nobody threw the food out: Biscuit ate it, so what he told Tam was wrong. Wanting a perfect score [1] and Biscuit hiding [4] each fit one clue only.
why.B: The note says "Dev will come Thursday" [1] and he is there on Thursday [7]. Kiran's idea that Dev threw out the food [3] is his wrong belief; Biscuit is "shy with new people" [1], but Dev was never there while she hid.

prompt.A: Part B: Which quotation from the text BEST supports the answer to Part A?
prompt.B: Part B: Which quotation from the story BEST supports your answer to Part A?

A: "Dev will come Thursday to water the plants." [1]
"Two green eyes watched him from the dark, then slid away." [4]
"Dev laughed and asked Kiran if the cat had won." [7]
"he planned to get a perfect score" [1]
B: "She won't touch anything I give her." [3]
"On Thursday, Dev was watering the plants when Mrs. Abara got home." [7]
"Biscuit is shy with new people, so don't take it personally." [1]
"Kiran heard someone at the door on Monday afternoon." [2]

why.A: Key: the note shows Dev could not have tossed the food on Monday [1], so the bowl was empty because Biscuit ate. The [4] line backs "talking will make Biscuit hide"; the "perfect score" line [1] backs "failed the job." "Dev laughed and asked Kiran if the cat had won" is unmatched: Dev never speaks in the story; the real line in [7] is "On Thursday, Dev was watering the plants when Mrs. Abara got home."
why.B: Key: Dev first appears on Thursday [7], as the note planned. The [3] line is Kiran's wrong belief that backs "threw out the food"; the [1] line backs "the reason she hid." "Kiran heard someone at the door on Monday afternoon" is unmatched: the story never says it and it backs "came by each day"; the real line in [2] is "Kiran filled the bowl and crouched by the couch."

prompt.A: Where did Biscuit spend Monday while Kiran was at school? Quote the sentence that shows it and give its paragraph number.
prompt.B: What does Kiran do differently on Wednesday evening from Monday and Tuesday? Quote the sentence that shows it and give its paragraph number.

answer.A: On the armchair: "That evening the bowl was empty, and the blanket on the armchair was warm and covered in orange hair." [3]
answer.B: He does not call her at all: "He forgot to call her at all." [5]

A: on the armchair blanket, with the [3] sentence about the warm blanket covered in orange hair
on the armchair, quoting "the blanket on the armchair was warm and covered in orange hair" [3]
B: he never calls her, quoting "He forgot to call her at all." [5]
he sits on the floor and studies, quoting "He sat on the floor with his back against the couch and opened his notebook." [5]

why.A: Full credit: the armchair (blanket) plus the [3] sentence. "Under the bed" is where she hides on Tuesday [4], not where she spent Monday. An answer with no quotation or paragraph-specific detail from the text earns at most half credit.
why.B: Full credit: he stops calling (or sits and studies) plus a [5] sentence. "He was quiet" with no line from [5] earns at most half credit.

questions.skill: find the detail that supports an inference

prompt.A: Which animal does the author use as an example of the small native animals that are harder to find where dingoes are rare?
prompt.B: What does the article say about the weather on the two sides of the fence?

A: bilbies
quolls
hopping mice
rock wallabies
B: Places on each side can have the same weather.
The sheep side can get far less rain than the dingo side.
Only one side floods.
The dingo side is wetter and cooler.

why.A: "...small native animals, such as hopping mice, are harder to find" [4]. The other three are real small Australian animals, but the article never names them; only a reader of [4] knows which one the author chose.
why.B: Scientists can compare places on the two sides that have "the same kind of land and the same weather" [2]. The barer ground [3] comes from kangaroos grazing, not from less rain; the floods [2] make gaps in the fence and are not said to fall on one side.

prompt.A: What does "cropped" mean as it is used in paragraph 3? Name the animals the paragraph says are doing it, and quote the sentence that tells you.
prompt.B: What does "slip" mean as it is used in paragraph 2? Tell when the paragraph says it happens, and quote the sentence that tells you.

answer.A: Bitten or eaten off short by grazing animals: the kangaroos. "Kangaroos graze on the same grass that sheep need." [3]
answer.B: To get past the fence without being stopped; it happens after floods leave gaps: "Still, a few slip through gaps after floods." [2]

why.A: Full credit: the meaning (eaten or bitten short) plus kangaroos and a [3] sentence. "Cut short" or "sheep ate it" with no line from [3] earns at most half credit; the sheep are on that side, but [3] names the kangaroos.
why.B: Full credit: the meaning (get past without being stopped) plus "after floods" and the [2] sentence. A meaning with no line or detail from [2] earns at most half credit.

A: eaten short by grazing kangaroos, quoting "Kangaroos graze on the same grass that sheep need." [3]
bitten off short by the many kangaroos on the side with few dingoes, quoting a [3] sentence about kangaroos
B: get past without being stopped, after floods, quoting "Still, a few slip through gaps after floods." [2]
sneak through gaps in the fence that floods make, quoting the [2] sentence

questions.skill: infer the author's purpose and point of view

prompt.A: Part A: Which statement best describes the author's view on what should happen to the fence?
prompt.B: Part A: Why does the author end paragraph 3 the way it does?

A: The author says it should stay until sheep can be kept safe another way.
The author says it should not change until scientists study it more.
The author never says so directly but hints it should come down.
The author does not say which side is right.
B: to explain why kangaroos are so much more common on the side where dingoes are rare
to show that more kangaroos also cause trouble for sheep ranchers
to show that both animals can live on the same plains peacefully
to show that the fence keeps the ranchers' sheep safe

why.A: Two steps: the author lists harms [3-4], then the good the fence does [5], reports both sides ("Some people say ... Others say") and says "None of this makes the answer simple" [5]. The call for more study is what "many scientists say" [5], not the author's own view, and the ending [6] says what the fence shows, not what to do.
why.B: The last sentence of [3] ties the kangaroo change back to the ranchers' sheep: more kangaroos eat the grass sheep need, so they compete; they do not live together peacefully. The cause of more kangaroos was given earlier in [3]; how the fence protects sheep comes in [5], not at the end of [3].

prompt.A: Part B: Which quotation from the text BEST supports the answer to Part A?
prompt.B: Part B: Which quotation from the article BEST supports your answer to Part A?

A: "None of this makes the answer simple." [5]
"Dingoes do kill sheep and calves." [5]
"more study is needed" [5]
"The plains need their dingoes back." [6]
B: "On the side with few dingoes, there are many more kangaroos." [3]
"Kangaroos and sheep feed side by side in peace." [3]
"Kangaroos graze on the same grass that sheep need." [3]
"For the families who raise sheep, the fence protects their living." [5]

why.A: Key: after giving both sides the author says the answer is not simple and picks neither [5]. "Dingoes do kill sheep and calves" [5] backs "should stay"; "more study is needed" [5] backs "wait for more study," but it is what many scientists say, not the author's view. "The plains need their dingoes back" is unmatched: it backs "hints it should come down," and the author never says it; the real line in [6] is "It shows how pulling one hunter out of a place can change far more than anyone planned."
why.B: Key: the sentence links more kangaroos to the grass sheep need [3]; they compete for it. The "many more kangaroos" line [3] backs "explain why kangaroos are common"; the families line [5] backs "the fence keeps sheep safe." "Kangaroos and sheep feed side by side in peace" is unmatched: the passage never says it and it backs "live together peacefully"; the real line in [3] is "Kangaroos graze on the same grass that sheep need," which shows they compete.

questions.skill: explain an idea with a quotation

prompt.A: In paragraph 2, the author calls the fence a natural experiment. Explain why it works as an experiment even though nobody planned it, and quote the sentence that shows it. Give the paragraph number.
prompt.B: In paragraph 5, what does the author admit to the people who want the fence to stay, and why does the author put it after the changes to the animals? Quote the sentence and give its paragraph number.

answer.A: Nobody built it as a test, but scientists can compare places on the two sides that have the same kind of land and the same weather, where only the number of dingoes differs: "Nobody set it up as a test, but scientists can compare places on the two sides that have the same kind of land and the same weather." [2]
answer.B: The author admits that dingoes do kill sheep and calves and that the fence protects ranch families' living. Coming after the harms in [3-4], it shows the question is not simple: "Dingoes do kill sheep and calves." [5] or "For the families who raise sheep, the fence protects their living." [5]

A: places on the two sides with the same land and weather can be compared, quoting the [2] sentence
nobody set it up but matching places on each side can be compared, quoting "Nobody set it up as a test..." [2]
B: dingoes kill sheep and calves, quoting [5], to show the answer is not simple
the fence protects ranchers' living, quoting [5], to balance the harms in [3-4]
"None of this makes the answer simple." [5] with what is admitted

why.A: Full credit needs both steps (nobody planned it; scientists can compare places on the two sides that have the same land and weather) and the [2] sentence. A general definition of an experiment with no line from [2] earns at most half credit.
why.B: Full credit needs what is admitted, why it comes after [3-4] (to show the choice is not simple), and a [5] sentence. A general claim with no line from [5] earns at most half credit.

sections.heading: CONSTRUCTED RESPONSE (4 points)
sections.directions: Write your answer on the lines.

prompt.A: How does Kiran change from the beginning of "Biscuit" to the end? Use RACE: R - Restate the question. A - Answer it. C - Cite two pieces of evidence with [paragraph numbers]. E - Explain how each piece of evidence proves your answer.
prompt.B: How does the way Kiran treats Biscuit change from Monday to Thursday? Use RACE: R - Restate the question. A - Answer it. C - Cite two pieces of evidence with [paragraph numbers]. E - Explain how each piece of evidence proves your answer.

answer.A: Kiran changes from trying hard and loudly to win Biscuit over to being calm and patient. At first he calls and taps the bowl, "louder each time" [2]. Later he "did not reach for her" and "hardly breathed" [6], and he asks to come back [7].
answer.B: Kiran goes from chasing Biscuit with noise to leaving her alone and letting her come to him. He shakes the bag and taps the bowl "louder each time" [2] and sings to her [4]; on Wednesday he "did not reach for her" [6] and asks to come back [7].

questions.why: Score with the RACE CHECKLIST. Strong evidence: [2] or [4] for the start; [5], [6] or [7] for the end. The Explain row needs how each quote shows the change.

rubric.title: RACE CHECKLIST
rubric.note: Score: Add the four rows and divide by 4. I round up.

criteria.name: Restate
levels: I turned the question into my first sentence.
I restated part of the question.
I copied the question word for word.

criteria.name: Answer
levels: I answered every part of the question clearly.
I answered, but part of my answer is unclear.
My answer only partly fits the question.
I did not answer the question.

criteria.name: Cite
levels: I used two quotes, each with a [paragraph number].
I used two quotes, but one has no [paragraph number].
I did not use any quotes.

criteria.name: Explain
levels: I explained how each quote proves my answer.
I said the quotes prove it but not how.
I did not explain my quotes.

facts.notes: Passage only (passage-p2.md, 'The Long Fence'). The teacher's notes cover sea otters and kelp, so no claim here has a teacher source; every claim was checked with web search (8 searches) and marked reference / off / judgment. Claims counted: [1] length >5,000 km; one of the longest structures; runs across the dry interior; ranchers built it; begun >100 years ago; purpose was to keep dingoes from sheep; dingoes are Australia's wild dogs. [2] fence mostly works; dingoes common on one side and rare on the other; a few get through gaps after floods; natural experiment; sites matched for land and weather. [3] many more kangaroos where dingoes are rare; dingoes hunt kangaroos and more young survive; grass cropped short and ground barer; kangaroos eat the grass sheep need. [4] foxes and cats brought by Europeans; dingoes kill foxes and cats; foxes more common where dingoes are rare; cats more common where dingoes are rare; hopping mice harder to find; foxes and cats a main cause of small-mammal losses. [5] dingoes kill sheep and calves; people disagree about removing the fence and many scientists call for more study. [6] built to solve one problem (dingoes eating sheep); removing one predator changed more than planned. 20 are reference-true. 1 is off: cats. 1 is overstated: the fence is credited alone. 2 are judgment calls for the teacher: the fence began as a rabbit fence, and paras [3]-[4] state a disputed cascade as settled fact. Sweep: the 'fence alone' cause sits in [2] and [6]. The cats claim appears only in [4], and the 'one problem' origin in [1] and [6]. The questions were not checked (they are being redesigned); recheck any question or key that uses cats, the fence-alone cause, or 'built to solve one problem'.

findings.where: The Long Fence [4]
findings.what: 'Where dingoes are rare, foxes and cats are more common' is overstated for cats. The fox part holds: foxes were more common where dingoes were absent (Letnic & Koch 2010, Letnic & Dworjanyn). The cat part does not hold everywhere: the main cross-fence comparison found feral cats did not respond to dingo exclusion (Letnic & Koch 2010), and only a later six-year SA study (2011-2017) found more cats on the dingo-free side. Direction: keep foxes as the firm claim and hedge cats. For example: 'Where dingoes are rare, foxes are more common, and some studies have found more feral cats too, and small native animals, such as hopping mice, are harder to find.' Or drop cats from this sentence. Facts to check: the wording should claim no more for cats than 'some studies'.
findings.source: Letnic & Koch 2010, Austral Ecology, 'Are dingoes a trophic regulator in arid Australia? A comparison of mammal communities on either side of the dingo fence' (https://trophiccascades.forestry.oregonstate.edu/sites/trophic/files/Letnic%20and%20Koch%202010.pdf); UNSW 2019, 'Dogged researchers show that dingoes keep feral cats in check' (https://www.unsw.edu.au/newsroom/news/2019/04/dogged-researchers-show-that-dingoes-keep-feral-cats-in-check)

findings.where: The Long Fence [2]
findings.what: 'The fence mostly works. Dingoes are common on one side and rare on the other.' credits the fence alone. Inside the fence, landholders are required by law to destroy wild dogs, by poison baiting (the main tool), trapping and shooting. The fence is a barrier, and the killing on the sheep side is a large part of why dingoes are rare there. This matters in a quiz on cause and effect: a student could infer that the fence alone emptied the area. Direction: add one sentence, for example 'On the sheep side, ranchers also poison, trap and shoot any dingoes they find.' Facts to check: baiting, trapping and shooting are all named in SA policy, and destroying wild dogs inside the fence is required by law in SA.

findings.where: The Long Fence [3]-[4]
findings.what: Paras [3]-[4] state the dingo, kangaroo/fox, grass/small-mammal chain as plain fact. Paras [3] and [4] each match published cross-fence studies. Whether dingoes control foxes and cats across Australia is disputed, however: Allen and colleagues found no rise in foxes or cats after dingo removal in baiting and fenced experiments, and other researchers dispute those methods. Para [5] says 'many scientists say more study is needed', which partly covers this. One reading: fine for grade 7, since [5] signals the uncertainty. The other: attribute the findings, e.g. '[3] Scientists who studied the fence found many more kangaroos...' This would also give the inference questions an author's-claim-versus-evidence angle. findings.where: The Long Fence [1]
findings.what: 'Ranchers began building it more than 100 years ago. They wanted to keep dingoes... away from their sheep.' The first sections (1880-1885) were built as rabbit fences, which failed and were converted section by section into a dingo barrier. Governments as well as landholders built and ran it. [6] says the same: 'built to solve one problem: dingoes eating sheep'. One reading: a fair grade 7 shortening, because the fence that exists today was made and kept up to stop dingoes, and '>100 years' is true under either date. This is not a known myth. The other reading: add 'Parts of it began as a fence against rabbits.' Teacher's call. Facts to check if added: rabbit-fence origin in the 1880s.

findings.where: The Long Fence [1]
findings.what: 'more than 5,000 kilometers long' and 'one of the longest structures on Earth' are true: about 5,614 km, and it is commonly described as one of the world's longest structures. 'Across the dry middle of Australia' is a fair shortening: the fence runs from southern Queensland to the Great Australian Bight through arid and semi-arid inland country, though not the Red Centre itself. Optional precision: 'across the dry outback'.

findings.where: The Long Fence [2]
findings.what: 'a few slip through gaps after floods' is true: state policy expects incursions after floods or fires, and wild dogs persist inside in places. 'natural experiment... same kind of land and the same weather' is a fair shortening: the studies compare matched sites, and the authors call the fence an inadvertent experiment. Rainfall and land use still differ somewhat between sides, which the satellite study notes. That detail is fine to leave out at grade 7.

findings.where: The Long Fence [3]
findings.what: All four claims check out. Kangaroos are far more abundant where dingoes are rare: one survey counted about 3,200 kangaroos and 1 dingo inside the fence, against 85 dingoes and 8 kangaroos outside. Dingoes prey mainly on kangaroos. Vegetation cover is lower where kangaroos are dense: kangaroo-exclusion plots inside the fence had about 12% more cover. Kangaroos compete with sheep for pasture. 'more young kangaroos live to grow up' is a fair simplification of predation on young kangaroos. Caution for the question writers: woody shrubs increase on the dingo-free side (UNSW 2016), so no question or key should say all plants decline there.
findings.source: Morris & Letnic 2017 (Nature news: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature.2017.21962); CSIRO Wildlife Research WR9920531 (https://www.publish.csiro.au/WR/WR9920531); UNSW 2016 shrub study (https://www.unsw.edu.au/newsroom/news/2016/12/detective-work-across-dingo-fence-reveals-new-factor-in-woody-sh)

findings.where: The Long Fence [4]
findings.what: These claims are true. Red foxes were brought from Europe for sport hunting, released in Victoria from about 1871. Feral cats came with European settlement. Dingoes kill foxes and cats, which is documented intraguild predation. The dusky hopping mouse is less abundant where dingoes are absent. Foxes and feral cats are the leading cause of Australia's small-mammal extinctions and range losses (Woinarski et al. 2015, PNAS), and 'a main reason' matches that. The one exception is the cats-more-common claim, which is FIX above.
findings.source: Tasmanian Government NRE, 'European Red Foxes' (https://nre.tas.gov.au/invasive-species/invasive-animals/invasive-mammals/european-red-foxes); Science News on Woinarski et al. 2015 (https://www.sciencenews.org/blog/wild-things/cats-and-foxes-are-driving-australias-mammals-extinct); Letnic & Koch 2010 (link above)

findings.what: 'Dingoes do kill sheep and calves' is true: sheep are the main livestock loss, and cattle losses are mostly calves. The split of opinion and the call for more study fairly reflect the real dispute (see the JUDGMENT on [3]-[4]). The paragraph gives both sides without taking one.
